## Proof that \(g\) is measurable

**Setup.** Let \(g:\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{C}\) be defined by \(g(re^{i\phi})=\ln r - i\phi\) with \(\phi\in(-\pi,\pi]\). We equip \(\mathbb{C}\cong\mathbb{R}^2\) with the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra. The only obstruction to continuity of \(g\) is the branch cut along the negative real axis, where \(\phi\) jumps from \(\pi\) to \(-\pi\).

**Step 1 — The rectangles \(R_n\) and injectivity of \(\exp\).**  
For \(n\ge 2\) define the compact rectangle
\[
R_n=[-n,n]\times\Bigl[-\pi+\tfrac1n,\;\pi-\tfrac1n\Bigr]\subset\mathbb{C}.
\]
The imaginary-part interval has length \(2\pi-\tfrac2n<2\pi\), so the exponential map \(\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)\) is **injective** on \(R_n\): if \(\exp w_1=\exp w_2\) with \(w_1,w_2\in R_n\), then \(e^{x_1}=e^{x_2}\) (so \(x_1=x_2\)) and the angles differ by a multiple of \(2\pi\), but both lie in an interval of length \(<2\pi\), forcing \(y_1=y_2\).

Since \(R_n\) is compact and \(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\) is Hausdorff, the continuous injection
\[
\exp\big|_{R_n}:R_n\longrightarrow U_n:=\exp(R_n)
\]
is a **homeomorphism** onto its (compact) image \(U_n\).

**Step 2 — \(g\) is continuous on each \(U_n\).**  
For \(z=re^{i\phi}\in U_n\) we have \((x,y)=(\ln r,\phi)\in R_n\) and \(z=\exp(x+iy)\). Hence
\[
g(z)=\ln r - i\phi = x - iy = \overline{(x+iy)}=\overline{\bigl(\exp|_{R_n}\bigr)^{-1}(z)}.
\]
Both \((\exp|_{R_n})^{-1}:U_n\to R_n\) (continuous, by Step 1) and complex conjugation \(\overline{(\cdot)}\) (continuous) are continuous, so
\[
g\big|_{U_n}=\overline{(\cdot)}\circ\bigl(\exp|_{R_n}\bigr)^{-1}
\]
is **continuous on \(U_n\)**.

**Step 3 — The open set \(V\) and the branch cut \(L\).**  
Let
\[
V=\bigcup_{n\ge 2}\exp\bigl(\operatorname{int}R_n\bigr)
=\bigl\{re^{i\phi}:r>0,\;\phi\in(-\pi,\pi)\bigr\}
=\mathbb{C}\setminus\bigl(\{0\}\cup L\bigr),
\]
where \(L:=\{re^{i\pi}:r>0\}=(-\infty,0)\times\{0\}\) is the negative real axis. Each \(\exp(\operatorname{int}R_n)\) is open (by the open mapping property / invariance of domain, or directly since \(\exp\) is a local homeomorphism), and \(g\) is continuous on each, with these open sets covering \(V\). Therefore **\(g|_V\) is continuous**.

The complement \(L=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\setminus V\) is closed in \(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\), hence **Borel**, and has two-dimensional Lebesgue measure \(0\) (it is a line).

**Step 4 — \(g\) is measurable on \(L\).**  
On \(L\), parameterize \(z=re^{i\pi}\) (\(r>0\)); then \(g(re^{i\pi})=\ln r-i\pi\), which is a continuous function of \(r\). Identifying \(L\cong(0,\infty)\) (a Borel space), \(g|_L\) is continuous, hence **Borel measurable**.

**Step 5 — Gluing.**  
For any Borel set \(B\subseteq\mathbb{C}\),
\[
g^{-1}(B)=\underbrace{\bigl(g|_V\bigr)^{-1}(B)}_{\text{Borel in }V\text{ (cts.)}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\bigl(g|_L\bigr)^{-1}(B)}_{\text{Borel in }L\text{ (meas.)}}.
\]
Since \(V\) is open (Borel) in \(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\) and \(g|_V\) is continuous, the first piece is Borel. Since \(L\) is Borel and \(g|_L\) is measurable, the second piece is Borel. Their union is Borel.

Thus \(g^{-1}(B)\) is Borel in \(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\) for every Borel \(B\subseteq\mathbb{C}\), i.e. **\(g\) is Borel measurable**. \(\blacksquare\)

**Remark.** The discontinuity along the branch cut \(L\) is harmless for measurability: \(L\) is a Borel set of measure zero, and on each side of it \(g\) agrees with a continuous branch (obtained via the homeomorphic inverse of \(\exp\) on the nested rectangles \(R_n\)). Countably many continuous pieces glued along a Borel null set preserve measurability.
